retagged.reason: The form 'оборотень' is printed in the nominative on afanasyev1869:p.529, but there in a Carinthian (хорутанскимъ) tale, and the page ties the word to no people. ralston1872:p.403 gives oboroten as the name for a person so changed 'in Russia', which the Russian row of sources/peoples.json fixes as Russians by context. Kept p.529 for the printed form and added p.403 for the people.

afanasyev1869:p.527 prints 'Волкодлакъ' as the head form of a list whose other forms carry language labels (малор., бѣлор., пол.), but prints no people term for the head form itself. ralston1872:p.404 renders the same list 'The Great-Russian volkodlak becomes, says Afanasief, in Little-Russian vovkulak...', and 'Great-Russian' is a table term for Russians. Kept p.527 for the printed form and added p.404 for the people.

afanasyev1869:p.532 prints 'О вовкулакахъ великорусскіе поселяне ... разсказываютъ', and 'великорусскіе' is a table term for Russians, so p.532 was added. People-table form added after verify (phase 4b-peoples-3): afanasyev1869:p.530 says 'По русскимъ повѣрьямъ, вовкулаки бываютъ двухъ родовъ' (by Russian beliefs, vovkulaki are of two kinds), and 'русскимъ' is now a form of the Russians row in sources/peoples.json, so the draft cite p.530 is restored. At first verify the form was missing from the table and p.530 was dropped.

grade_rationale.text: Afanasyev records vovkulaki among Great-Russian peasants and, as involuntary werewolves, in the Ukraine and White Russia.
Afanasyev also records the belief among the Poles and the Serbs.
Ralston's account of involuntary werewolves, with the Polish, White-Russian and Ruthenian tales and the black-dog cure, cites Afanasyev, so it is counted with him, not as a second source.
Ralston's Ukrainian pitchfork tradition also cites Afanasyev.

Ralston independently gives oboroten as the name in Russia for a person changed by magic, records the Russian peasant belief in bristles under the werewolf's tongue, and prints a werewolf spell from Sakharov.
Machal, a third author, records the Vlkodlak among the Slavs generally, with South-Slav and Istrian traditions.
